news.title: US Sen. Marsha Blackburn wins GOP nomination for Tennessee governor
news.text:
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn won Tennessee's Republican nomination for governor on Aug. 6, defeating two other conservative candidates and cementing her status as the heavy favorite to become the first woman to lead the state, NBC News and the Associated Press have projected.

"One year ago, we set out on this journey with one goal: to make Tennessee America's conservative leader and show the nation what strong, bold, conservative leadership looks like." Blackburn posted on X shortly before 9:30 pm ET. "Tonight, I am humbled and honored that you've chosen me as your Republican nominee for Governor."

In November's midterm, Blackburn will face Jerri Green, who won the Democratic nomination, CNN and the Associated Press projected.

But it will be a massive uphill battle for Green, a Memphis council member. A Democrat has not sat in the state's governor seat since former Gov. Phil Bredesen was termed out in 2011 after his 2006 victory, and Republican candidates have dominated the state in recent years. 

Blackburn, 74, entered the Republican primary race the clear favorite over U.S. Rep. John Rose and state Rep. Monty Fritts, at one point holding double-digital leads in early polling. She is popular among Republicans and was the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate from Tennessee, currently serving her second Senate term after four terms in the U.S. House of Representatives.

President Donald Trump did not endorse a candidate for the Republican primary, although Blackburn and Rose are both strong supporters of the president. Trump swept the state in 2024 with an almost 30-point-lead over Kamala Harris.

Blackburn's goal is "to make Tennessee America’s conservative leader," according to her campaign Twitter, and her campaign spotlights her commitment to Trump, his "America First Agenda" and the Make America Great Again movement.

On the issues, her campaign advocated for core-Republican platforms such as economic growth through tax cuts, fighting crime and illegal immigration, cutting wasteful government spending, parental rights and removing "woke" curriculums from schools.

"She fights every day for President Donald Trump’s America First agenda, to keep men out of girls’ sports, hold big tech accountable, defend life, protect American farmland from Communist China, secure our borders, and deport all illegal aliens," Blackburn's website says.

Blackburn's campaign also gained national attention when she released a July campaign video where the senator sat in a Chinese food restaurant crumbling Fortune cookies to show "how hard am I going to crack down on China." She also faced criticism for not debating her two primary opponents.

The race tightened as the primary neared but Blackburn stayed in the lead until her final victory.

Rose's campaign contrasted Blackburn's, pointing to his family roots as an eighth-generation farmer in the state and highlighting that he is "not a career politician." Similar to Blackburn, though, he relied on a connection to Trump, calling himself an "unapologetic supporter" of the president who will align with Trump's "blueprint." He focused on five campaign priorities – education, infrastructure, healthcare, energy and economic and community development.

Fritts ran a small-government "liberty & less government" campaign that called for 10 pillars including eliminating a grocery sales tax, defending the Second Amendment, supporting voter ID laws and removing incentives that attracted "illegal aliens" to the state.

On the Democratic side, two candidates besides Green – Carnita Atwater and Tim Cyr – were on the primary ballot. Green campaigned on supporting working families, strengthening public schools, expanding Medicaid in rural parts of the state, "common-sense" gun laws and clean climate preservation.

This is a developing story.

Contributing: Vivian Jones, The Tennessean

news.title: Guest Opinion: Once again, national Democrats are making a primary mistake
news.text:
It is clear in hindsight, and was clear to many at the time, that the choice to sideline New Hampshire in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary process was designed to spare President Joe Biden from scrutiny over his ability to mount a vigorous reelection campaign. South Carolina was chosen to go first.

As New Hampshire, following state law, held its primary first anyway, there was a farcical super-PAC effort by Biden surrogates to win the write-in vote here without Biden campaigning. As that succeeded, the New Hampshire delegates were seated at the Democratic convention.

Now it seems clear that New Hampshire will be passed over again by Democrats, based on the premise that it is not diverse enough, in favor of South Carolina or Nevada. The former would be a very strange proving ground. Biden got only 43.4 percent of the South Carolina vote in 2020, even as he went on to win nationally. There is just one Democrat in the state’s seven-member House delegation. The state legislature has been Republican since 1998.

Nevada is also a peculiar political ecosystem. It was there that President Donald Trump, as a candidate, unveiled his June 2024 “no tax on tips” proposal, which Kamala Harris parroted at a Nevada rally two months later, and that led to a four-year suspension of taxes on tips in the federal budget reconciliation bill that passed last year.

If Nevada goes first, a successful Democratic candidate will have to appeal to the critical bloc of Culinary Workers Union members, which could shape his or her remaining campaign in ways that may not appeal to the broader nation. It reminds me of the ethanol pledge that “The West Wing” so well depicted presidential candidates Arnold Vinick and Matt Santos struggling with at a Corn Growers Expo in Iowa.

There is no such organized group to pander to in New Hampshire. And yet, for those who might suggest our state lacks the diversity to go first, I would ask what one’s definition of diversity is. Isn’t age a demographic? New Hampshire has the nation’s second-oldest population. Nationally, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, “From 2020 to 2024, the older population grew by 13.0 percent, significantly outpacing the 1.4 percent growth of working-age adults (ages 18 to 64), while the number of children declined by 1.7 percent.”

By 2034, U.S. sales of adult diapers are projected to exceed baby diaper sales. Our aging population is going to place a strain on safety net programs like Medicaid and Medicare, and New Hampshire would be a great place to hone a message to senior voters. After all, according to the trustees of the Medicare Hospital Insurance trust fund, it will be insolvent by 2033. Kind of a big deal.

There are an estimated 4 million tipped workers in the country. In contrast, in 2024 data showed that 43.3 million U.S. citizens who are 65-and-older voted, easily the biggest age demographic to vote. It might be somewhat important for a Democratic candidate to win over these older voters, given that Trump won them 51-47 percent over Harris.

Treating New Hampshire as flyover country would also be taking for granted a state where Republicans have a lock on state government and the presidential vote isn’t a given. Had Al Gore won New Hampshire in 2000, Florida would have been immaterial. Although Hillary Clinton lost the electoral college in 2016, she nearly lost New Hampshire too — carrying it by only a 47.6 percent-47.2 percent margin over Trump.

Finally, the retail politics required to win the New Hampshire primary, instead of just pouring money into a major media market like Las Vegas, has made for more nimble candidates in both political parties. It would be a shame for national Democrats to devalue that tradition. And it would be a big loss to the civic experience of Granite Staters.

news.title: ‘Uncommitted’ founder Alawieh who pushed Democrats to vote against Biden over Gaza wins primary
news.text: Abbas Alawieh, a founder of the Uncommitted movement that pressured former US president Joe Biden to change his Israel policy, is the projected winner of a Democratic primary for Michigan's state Senate. Alawieh rose to national prominence as a key architect of the campaign to withhold votes from Biden during Michigan's presidential primary in 2024, a protest against the administration's support for Israel as it inflicted mounting casualties in Gaza. Alawieh defeated state representative Erin Byrnes in Tuesday's primary to represent Michigan's 2nd Senate District, a heavily Arab-American area covering Dearborn and parts of Detroit - and the epicenter of the Uncommitted effort. He won 59% of the vote to Byrnes' 41% after more than 95% of votes were counted, according to the Associated Press, and is now almost certain to win the solid-blue state Senate seat in November. Alawieh, who was born in Lebanon and grew up in Dearborn, acknowledged his victory without giving a speech on Wednesday. His staff announced that Alawieh's maternal grandfather, Hajj Kassem Bazzi, died Tuesday night as they awaited the election results. “Please keep Abbas's family in your prayers as they take needed time together,” Alawieh's team said in a statement. “Abbas will share his own thoughts on the race soon. For now, thank you to every community that made this win possible.”Alawieh was backed by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. He previously worked as a staffer for congressional Democrats, including Michigan Rep. Rashida Tlaib, former Michigan Rep. Andy Levin, and former Missouri rep. Cori Bush, who lost a primary against Rep. Wesley Bell on Tuesday. Over 100,000 vote for 'uncommitted' in 2024 Democratic primaryAlawieh, alongside Layla Elabed, co-founded the campaign urging Michigan Democrats to vote “uncommitted” in the 2024 Democratic presidential primary. The movement attracted a groundswell of support, including from some Jews, and won more than 100,000 votes, or 13% of the overall vote. Biden was beaten by the uncommitted vote in Dearborn, where Arab Americans make up more than half the population.The Uncommitted movement also spread to other states, rallying more than 650,000 voters nationwide, and crystallized a lack of enthusiasm for Biden, who eventually stepped off the presidential ticket.Alawieh served as one of the Uncommitted delegates at the 2024 Democratic National Convention, where he and other delegates unsuccessfully lobbied to place a Palestinian speaker on the agenda. Alawieh did not make Israel and Gaza a central part of his campaign for the state Senate seat, instead focusing on supporting working families and investing in healthcare, housing, public transit, and education. Still, he told the Michigan Advance in February that his role in the Uncommitted movement resonated with people in his district. “For the people in real life - not on Twitter - it is clear to them that parties' focus on prioritizing funding for war crimes was out of touch with what voters wanted,” he said. “The party was undoubtedly wrong about Gaza in 2024.” Kamala Harris mends fences with Abbas AlawiehWhile some Democrats blamed the Uncommitted campaign for contributing to US President Donald Trump's defeat of former vice president Kamala Harris, who lost Michigan in her 2024 presidential run, Alawieh and Harris have mended fences enough to recently sit down for a meeting.Harris “initiated” the meeting after months of phone calls, Alawieh said in July. “I urge VP Harris and all of our party's leaders to side with peace-loving Americans against endless wars, in opposition to the Israeli military's genocide in Gaza, and against the ethnic cleansing campaign in Lebanon,” he said. Alawieh has said that he voted for Harris against Trump in the 2024 general election, while Elabed did not.The centrality of Israel in Michigan's primaries has spawned bitter divides between Jewish Democrats and others in the party concerning the threat of antisemitism. In one incident that shook Detroit-area Jews earlier this year, Temple Israel in the suburb of West Bloomfield was rammed by a truck laden with explosives. The man who drove the truck, a US citizen from Lebanon, had recently lost several family members in an Israeli airstrike on Lebanon. Alawieh responded to the attack by declaring his support for Jewish Michiganders.“We must stand in unequivocal defense of the humanity and safety of our Jewish siblings and denounce this heinous act,” he said in a statement. “My family and I are praying for safety for communities across our state who are feeling afraid right now, and we are holding our Jewish community members extra close.”

news.title: At the Races: Crossing lines
news.text:
Welcome to At the Races! Each week we bring you news and analysis from the CQ Roll Call campaign team. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

By Daniela Altimari and Mary Ellen McIntire

Poll after poll suggests Americans are deeply split along partisan lines on most key issues. Signs of that abound, whether in the halls of Congress or on the midterm campaign trail. 

Yet this week brought glimmers of hope for those who believe that finding common ground across rigid political boundaries is healthy for democracy.

In Arizona, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs plans to select a former Republican mayor as her running mate, The New York Times reported. 

Hobbs, a vulnerable purple-state incumbent vying for a second term against Republican Rep. Andy Biggs, is expected to pick John Giles, who was mayor of the Phoenix suburb of Mesa, and recently switched his party registration to “no party preference,’’ the Times reports. Giles has a history of bucking his now-former party; in 2024, he backed Democrats Kamala Harris for president and Ruben Gallego for Senate.

Meanwhile, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Democrat running for a second term in another pivotal battleground state, picked up the backing this week of two Republican mayors from South Georgia and a prominent Arizona Republican: former Sen. Jeff Flake.

“I’m still a conservative Republican,’’ Flake told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution. “But character matters. And I want someone in that seat who takes the institution seriously and will protect the institution.”

In Texas, former Tarrant County Judge Glen Whitley, a Republican, endorsed Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. Whitley had previously announced his opposition to Talarico’s GOP opponent, state Attorney General Ken Paxton. 

“Ken Paxton has spent years embarrassing Texas. He’s known for scandal, indictment, infidelity and putting his own interests ahead of Texans,’’ Whitley said in a radio ad that aired in June.

There haven’t been as many prominent defections among Democrats, but last month, Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo picked up the support of 130 Democrats who are helping to burnish his moderate credentials as he seeks a second term. 

President Donald Trump himself has a history of forging political partnerships with prominent erstwhile Democrats, including former Hawaii Rep. Tulsi Gabbard and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a scion of one of the most celebrated families in Democratic politics.

Bipartisan goodwill, though, only gets you so far. Former Georgia Republican Lt. Gov. Geoff Duncan drew praise from Democrats for backing Harris in 2024. But when he tried to run for governor as a Democrat this year, he couldn’t break even 10 percent of the vote.

Starting gate

Election night recap: Abdul El-Sayed clinched the Democratic Senate nomination in Michigan, narrowly defeating Rep. Haley Stevens in a divisive primary that the party is trying to move on from. Republicans have already begun attacking their newly minted opponent as sympathetic to terrorists and “dangerous” for the swing state. Meanwhile, Missouri Rep. Wesley Bell defeated a comeback attempt from former Rep. Cori Bush, handing progressives a loss on an otherwise mostly good night for Democrats’ left flank. And over the weekend, Del. Stacey Plaskett claimed the Democratic nod for governor of the U.S. Virgin Islands, while Guam Del. James C. Moylan survived a Republican primary challenge, our colleague Nick Eskow reported.

Edwards out: Embattled Rep. Chuck Edwards announced he was ending his reelection bid after the House Ethics Committee recommended the North Carolina Republican be censured for engaging in “persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct” toward two female staffers. Edwards said he’ll serve out the remainder of his term.

Keeping their distance: House Republicans are keeping their distance from their Ohio colleague Max Miller, who is facing allegations of domestic abuse, Roll Call’s Nina Heller reports. Meanwhile, the House Ethics Committee announced it would investigate allegations of domestic violence and abuse and illegal drug use against Miller after he publicly called for the panel to look into him, saying he had “absolutely nothing to hide.”

Redistricting restart: Maryland voters will vote on a constitutional amendment this November that, if approved, would clear the way for Democratic legislators to redraw the state’s congressional map. New lines would almost certainly target Rep. Andy Harris, Maryland’s only Republican in Congress. 

DCCC expands the map again: In a move that reflects their growing confidence ahead of the midterms, House Democrats are zeroing in on 12 additional GOP targets in deep-red districts, nearly all of which Trump carried by double digits in 2024. The new targets include the North Carolina district of NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson. The NRCC dismissed the announcement, saying Democrats were entering "the hallucination phase of the election cycle.” 

Dakota departure: The Democratic Senate nominee in South Dakota ended his campaign following calls from party activists to exit the race and leave independent Brian Bengs as the main competitor against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Julian Beaudion’s decision follows similar recent moves by Democrats in deep-red Nebraska and Idaho. 

RIP: Former House Appropriations Chairwoman Kay Granger, the first Republican woman to lead the powerful spending committee, drew bipartisan praise following her death Sunday at 83, our colleague Aidan Quigley reported. The Texan became chairwoman of the Appropriations panel after Republicans won the House during the 2022 midterms. She stepped down in 2024, a year when she was largely absent from Congress as her family reported she was suffering from dementia.

Guv roundup: Gubernatorial matchups were set in two key states that held primaries Tuesday. In battleground Michigan, Republican Rep. John James will take on Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson in the race to succeed term-limited Democrat Gretchen Whitmer. In Kansas, Republican hopes of flipping the governorship rest with state Senate President Ty Masterson, who will face Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher. Meanwhile, in Mississippi, Attorney General Lynn Fitch is hoping to become the Magnolia State’s first female governor, launching her 2027 campaign this week. 

#TN05: Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee endorsed Charlie Hatcher, the former state agriculture commissioner who is challenging GOP Rep. Andy Ogles, in Thursday’s primary. Hatcher also has the backing of Lee’s predecessor, Bill Haslam, though Ogles has the all-important Trump endorsement. The president has endorsed in all House races, save for the open 6th District, which Rep. John W. Rose is vacating to run for governor. 

#FL07: Florida Reps. Anna Paulina Luna and Mike Haridopolos endorsed former news anchor Ryan Elijah’s primary challenge to fellow GOP Rep. Cory Mills, who is the subject of an Ethics Committee investigation. 

Democratic endorsements: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is backing Democrat Katy Padilla Stout in Texas’ 23rd District. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill's Mission to Deliver PAC is endorsing 13 congressional hopefuls with military or national security backgrounds. They include candidates facing upcoming primaries such as Massachusetts Rep. Seth Moulton, who is challenging Sen. Edward J. Markey; Marine Corps veteran Maura Sullivan, who’s running for New Hampshire’s open 1st District; and Navy veteran and former NASA Chief of Staff Bale Dalton, who's seeking Florida's 7th District held by Republican Cory Mills.

#MESEN: Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC with ties to Senate Democratic leaders, released a poll Thursday that found Democrat Troy Jackson leading Maine Sen. Susan Collins, 49 percent to 45 percent with 6 percent undecided. The polling memo said that this year, Collins faces “a much more hostile political environment than she did in 2020.”

Missouri redistricting: Opponents of Missouri’s new GOP-drawn congressional map are suing after the Republican secretary of state blocked an effort to let voters weigh in on the new lines this fall, saying the challenge was unconstitutional. 

What we're reading

#FLSEN: Sen. Ashley Moody’s campaign to complete the Senate term she was appointed to last year when Marco Rubio became secretary of state is more low key than the races being run by other top Florida Republicans, Politico reports, and that has sparked some concerns by GOP operatives. Democrats hope that Alex Vindman, who has proved to be a strong fundraiser, can force a competitive race this fall.

Who will win the "orphaned" vote? Due to California’s nonpartisan primary system, the general elections in several key House races are one-party affairs, including the contest for the redrawn 40th District between Republican Reps. Young Kim and Ken Calvert. The Los Angeles Times looks at the strategic decisions “orphaned” Democratic voters are making about who to support. 

“Survival mode”: The Associated Press takes stock of DNC Chair Ken Martin as he fights to hold on to his job amid mounting frustration over how he handled a 2024 election “autopsy” report and the party’s financial struggles.

Courting Black conservatives: Capital B News examines Georgia Republican Rep. Mike Collins’ effort to win over Black voters in his challenge to Sen. Jon Ossoff. Collins’ quest comes as “questions about a member of his family’s white nationalist views – and the candidate’s own social media history – continue to generate negative headlines," the outlet reports.

An aging donor: The New York Times reports that Ronald Lauder, the cosmetics heir who has been a major donor for New York Republicans, seems to have cut off his political spending, raising questions within the state GOP of who might match his giving.

The count: 35 percent

That’s the share of Americans who profess to have no opinion on their district’s current candidates for Congress, according to a new Economist/YouGov poll.

That perhaps shouldn’t be surprising, given that 72 House districts – home to a total of nearly 36 million registered voters – won’t have an incumbent on the November ballot. That’s largely due to the abnormally high number of members willingly leaving the chamber, either to retire or seek other office, as well as those who resigned or lost their primaries.

In addition, redistricting in multiple states this cycle has thrown millions more voters in newly redrawn districts with a different House incumbent atop their ballot.– By Roll Call’s Ryan Kelly

Key race: #WI03

Candidates: Wisconsin GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden’s 3rd District seat is a top Democratic target this fall. National Democrats have largely lined up behind Rebecca Cooke, who unsuccessfully challenged Van Orden in 2024 and lost a Democratic primary for the seat in 2022. Also seeking the Democratic nomination is former Eau Claire City Council President Emily Berge. 

Why it matters: The battleground 3rd District is likely to be among the most competitive races this November, but Cooke, Democrats’ preferred candidate, must first get through Tuesday’s primary.

Cash dash: Cooke has been the race’s top fundraiser so far, bringing in $8.6 million through July 22, when she reported having $1.8 million on hand. Berge raised $729,000 and had $106,000 banked for the campaigns’ final stretch. Van Orden, meanwhile, reported raising $7.5 million this cycle and had $4.7 million on hand when he filed his pre-primary report last month. Outside groups have been active in the race over the past year. Law Enforcement for a Safer America PAC has spent $47,000 to support Van Orden, while the Wisco Project PAC, which mobilizes college students in the state, has spent $58,000 opposing his campaign. Pro-Choice Majority Action has spent $249,000 on ads supporting Cooke. And the Indivisible Project dropped $2,290 on a pro-Berge billboard. Meanwhile, Cooke has requested an extension on her personal financial disclosure that OpenSecrets reports has drawn criticism from both Berge and Van Orden.

Backers: The DCCC is backing Cooke, adding her to its Red to Blue program for promising candidates earlier this year. She’s also won endorsements from across the ideological spectrum, from the moderate Blue Dog PAC to progressives such as Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and home-state Sen. Tammy Baldwin. Berge touts endorsements from several local leaders and the local Indivisible Coalition. Van Orden, as the incumbent, is backed by the traditional Republican groups. 

What they’re saying: In the Democratic primary, Berge has advocated more progressive policies such as “Medicare for All,” while Cooke said at a June forum that while she supports a public option, steps like restoring expired health insurance subsidies were a more likely approach for Democrats in Congress. Cooke has run ads highlighting her endorsement from Sanders, while another recent spot claims Van Orden “sold us out” on data centers. While Berge is the underdog in the primary, her campaign argues it’s gained momentum ahead of Tuesday’s primary and sees a path to victory. Van Orden, who hasn’t had to contend with a primary, has trained his attacks on Cooke, saying that she’s Democrats' "anointed" candidate and that he’s brought back important resources for the state as a member of Congress.

Terrain: The 3rd District is largely rural, covering parts of southwestern and western Wisconsin, including the cities Eau Claire and La Crosse. Trump carried the seat by 7 points in 2024, while Van Orden defeated Cooke by 3 points to win a second term. Inside Elections rates the race a Toss-up.

Wild cards: The 3rd District has become a popular destination for members of Trump’s Cabinet, many of whom have made appearances in the district this year, Politico reported. And a win for Francesca Hong in next week’s gubernatorial primary could complicate things for down-ballot Democrats trying to maintain some distance from the self-described democratic socialist, Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales wrote last week.

Tennessee is a rare state that holds its primaries on Thursdays for largely unknown reasons, and all eyes will be on Republican Rep. Andy Ogles as he faces off against his better-funded challenger. Meanwhile, Sen. Marsha Blackburn confronts Rep. John W. Rose and state Rep. Monty Fritts in her pursuit of the GOP seal of approval for her gubernatorial bid. And the Republican primaries for two open House seats – the GOP-held 6th District and newly deep-red 9th – will likely determine their next members of Congress. 

Photo finish

Former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford, with pigs in tow, returned to the State House in Columbia on Thursday to protest wasteful spending in the US government. The former congressman is running in next week’s special primary to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham on the GOP ticket. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

news.title: Is 'Communist' No Longer a Slur?
news.text:
It is not difficult, these days, to see the neo-communist flipside of "Democratic Socialists" — once they find power.

Indeed, the more the ossified Democratic Party claims that its growing cadre of socialist renegades are not really socialists, the more they act like — and even appear comfortable being called — communists.

With every new policy they propose, the socialists have been dropping the pretense that they are not Marxists.

How about declaring capitalism a failure?

All the socialists now do that — and even Democratic California Governor Gavin Newsom has also started agreeing that "capitalism as we know it doesn't work either." Oddly, Newsom himself, a multimillionaire and a beneficiary of arch-capitalist Gordon Getty's largesse, seems to have done quite well under capitalism.

Confiscating private property?

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani claims he will do just that if New York's landlords, in his opinion, are poor custodians of their own property.

Dismantling the U.S. Constitution?

Almost all Democrats have long called for destroying the 238-year-old Electoral College. And now the socialists openly brag that, when they take over the Democratic Party and then the nation, they will, as good Bolsheviks, go much further: destroying the Senate, destroying the Pentagon, destroying prisons, destroying the police, and destroying our borders.

And they want to take over utilities, break up or absorb corporate agriculture, and own major industries. Apparently, socialists believe that with a snap of their fingers they can destroy key elements of the U.S. constitutional order. Would these "socialists" even resent their agenda being called "communist"?

They also seem to have taken their cue for such radical change from "mainstream" Democrats — for example, Kamala Harris. Now in her third vain bid for the presidency, she has adopted the doctrine of "if you can't beat them, join them." So Harris now promises that if she is elected, she will pack the court, admit two new blue states (to snag four liberal senators), end the filibuster, and junk the Electoral College. How she plans to amend the Constitution to that effect she never tells us.

Like all good Marxists, these "ends-justify-the-means" leftists show an utter lack of principle: If two new red states wished to join the U.S., they would lecture us on the sanctity of a 50-state union. If they were a permanent Senate minority, they would, as in the past, honor the filibuster. If they had lost the popular vote in two recent elections but won the Electoral College, they would praise the wisdom of the Founders. If they had their Earl Warren-era majority again, they would laud the continuity of the 157-year-old nine-justice Supreme Court.

How about making "enemies of the people" lists and forcing sales of private property?

Mamdani just sent out a public list of nearly one million New York homeowners. He sent official warnings to 17,000 of these property owners that, if within four weeks they cannot prove that they have lived full-time in their own properties, the city will levy a huge surtax on them to drive home the point that no one should own an additional high-value home. Are show trials next for those who decline to reply?

In other words, Mamdani has flipped the American tradition of "innocent until proven guilty." Instead, almost 20,000 New Yorkers are now automatically presumed guilty of being house-hoarding, capitalist leeches who owe the exploited classes tens of thousands of dollars a year in reparations, unless they — the newly presumed guilty — can prove themselves innocent.

Welcome to Mamdani's revolutionary court.

Mamdani's new surtax could add from $40,000 to $350,000 a year to tens of thousands of homeowners' taxes — in addition to already-existing steep property taxes that often range from $5,000 to $150,000.

Most owners will do the math and see that the new aggregate tax payouts in just a few years could be more than the value of the home itself.

Why is Mamdani doing this?

The socialist mayor's aim here seems twofold:

First, he wants to flush out and dox anyone owning two homes as a purported enemy of the people.

And so, Mamdani created a list of his targets, including their addresses, and published it. To the extent that many properties really were second homes, Mamdani has now made sure that all New Yorkers, including envious rubberneckers, would-be squatters, and hardened criminals, know exactly where they might target a sometimes-vacant home.

Second, he wants to force a massive fire sale of second homes that would crash home values in general and so redistribute now "affordable" houses to those whom Mamdani considers, as victims of capitalism, to be more deserving of these properties.

Recently, on cable news, the national co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, Megan Romer, was asked a series of questions about her group's published agenda. Far from denying its communist radicalism, she gleefully confirmed it all — from destroying the border to ending prisons, the military, and the police.

But it is in Spain, and Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's corrupt and unpopular regime, where we see what one-eyed-jack socialists can do when they are finally in power, especially when they are hated and on their way out.

Sanchez has given amnesty to 600,000 illegal aliens. One result was that 60,000 Muslim men from North Africa in a single day recently swarmed Spain's colonial outpost on the Moroccan coast at Ceuta, demanding amnesties and free subsidized passes into European Spain — while looting and vandalizing businesses and attacking Spaniards.

So why do European socialists and American leftists, once elected, destroy borders, create conditions of mass chaos, and welcome in millions of illegal aliens — poor, often angry, and unassimilated — from the Third World?

Aside from their belief that the capitalists and their bourgeois hirelings deserve chaos, violence, and upheaval, they hate the fact that capitalism is too class-fluid to furnish a permanent exploited proletarian underclass.

And so they import a huge victim class, and virtue signal their purported moral superiority. Then they spend lavish social largesse upon the influx, and, in quid pro quo fashion, thus bind their imported underclass with their welfare-state assurances.

Mail-in and early ballots, no-ID voting, same-day registration, ballot harvesting and curing, and no final verdicts on Election Day were all leftist projects, all designed to enroll as many illegal voters as possible.

The Left has also learned from experience that the time between immigrant parents fleeing third-world hellholes to find safety, freedom, and prosperity in the U.S. and their children hating the very generous host that welcomed them — and demanding that America be radically transformed to resemble the catastrophe from which they or their parents fled — is often only about 20 years.

So if one enjoys watching the careers of Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, AOC, or Mamdani, then one should certainly vote socialist to ensure that they are the new model for American elected officials.

It is the paradox of our age that anyone can flee Somalia, the West Bank, Puerto Rico, or Uganda and then win the global lottery by being accepted into America's constitutional society and free-market economy — only to do their best to repay the generosity of their host by turning their new country into something unrecognizable to the prior 10 generations of Americans.

But then again, America might become quite similar to the mess they abandoned.

So far, the model holds true: Socialist candidates (as opposed to registered socialist activists) hide their communist-adjacent agendas during elections. news.title: Now We Have Proof the Democrats' Anti-Trump Lawfare Was Never About the Law
news.text:
Long before Donald Trump took the oath of office for his second term — heck, before he was even reelected — Democrat state attorneys general were already building the machine designed to stop him.

Seven attorneys general signed the agreement on April 28, 2024. Thirteen more joined in May and June.

The pact was called "Privileged & Confidential Common Interest Agreement." It was built to do exactly what it sounds like: Keep the states' coordination hidden from the public and from anyone who might dare oppose them in court. The signers said they wanted to pursue their shared legal interests "while avoiding any waiver of the confidentiality of those privileged materials." Translation: Total secrecy while colluding against a sitting president who hadn't even taken office yet.

To me, the most significant part of this pact is that Biden was still in the race when the first signatures went on that agreement in April 2024. He wouldn't drop out for nearly three months. The sitting Democrat president was telling the country he intended to serve another term, the party was acting like he was going to win, all while Democrat attorneys general were already plotting to stop Trump upon his inevitable return to office.

ICYMI: Did a Democrat Senator Accidentally Admit He Knows That Fauci Broke the Law?

The coalition had already divided up legal research by topic, built a shared "brief bank" of pre-drafted briefs, and pored over the Project 2025 policy blueprint hunting for lawsuit targets. Trump hadn't signed a bill. He hadn't issued an executive order. He hadn't taken any official action as president, because he wasn't president yet. None of that mattered. The lawsuits were already being written.

Since Trump's second term began, Democrat attorneys general have sued his administration close to 100 times. California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D-Calif.) has taken part in 82 of those lawsuits. Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser (D-Colo.) has joined at least 75. Washington Attorney General Nick Brown (D-Wash.) has joined 70.

Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown (D-Md.) claims the early coordination was reasonable preparation once Trump's nomination looked inevitable, but this confirms that the strategy was always about resistance, not the rule of law.

Former Utah Attorney General Mark Shurtleff, a Republican who now often votes for Democrats, called the secrecy “not normal at all."

New Jersey tucked $1 million into its fiscal year 2026 budget just to fund two new staff positions dedicated to the coalition's work. That’s right, taxpayers are literally footing the bill for a legal ambush that was planned before Trump even won the election. Imagine all the other things California could have wasted more money on. Democrats can claim all they want that this is about accountability and the rule of law, but it’s just blanket resistance.

And if you live in a blue state, you’re paying for it.

news.title: What Gen Z’s dark humor really says about their values
news.text:
After Luigi Mangione was arrested in December 2024 in connection with the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, the internet did what it often does: It turned something serious into a joke.

Although Mangione has pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder in New York and to federal stalking charges, viral memes at the time romanticized him as a popular – and incredibly attractive – man of the people who made corporate elites within the American health insurance industry afraid.

Some of these memes adhered to conventional forms of political satire. One, for example, quoted a speech from the movie “A Bug’s Life,” in which a villainous grasshopper argues for the need to punish the movie’s ant protagonist to keep the other ants in line. In this meme, the political point was clear: Elites preserve power by making examples of insignificant ants who dare to challenge them.

The point was less clear with other memes, including celebrations of Mangione’s fashion-forward shackled ankles in court and mock Burger King advertisements referencing the fact that a McDonald’s employee had been the one to call law enforcement on him: “Burger King: We won’t turn you in to the Feds.” Rather than being ironic, they are unserious.

Nonetheless, memes like those received serious reactions from social commentators and political pundits who interpreted them as evidence that America’s young adults are nihilistic and morally indifferent.

As an experimental psychologist who studies moral judgments about real-world controversies, I have examined these attitudes toward Mangione and the humor surrounding him online.

I believe these reactions are better understood not as a rejection of value but as a refusal to participate in conversations that feel selective and disconnected from young people’s broader economic and political frustrations. In my assessment, Gen Z’s dark and nonsensical humor does not show a lack of moral values, but it’s instead the product of its desire to engage in more authentic conversations about what they believe.

Research shows deep levels of alienation among Gen Z, or young adults born between 1997 and 2012. Having grown up with smartphones and social media, this generation has come of age in an increasingly online world. Despite the internet’s capacity for instantaneous interaction, followers have proved a poor replacement for friends.

Gen Z is among the most socially isolated and psychologically distressed generations on record. Compared with prior generations, fewer friendships and romantic relationships have left many young adults craving connection and solidarity. This alienation is also evident in their skepticism toward institutions and traditional narratives about values.

Many are pessimistic about achieving the American Dream and question the value of higher education. What was once considered the optimal vehicle for living a better life is instead viewed as a barrier.

If the American Dream feels out of reach, and college seems like an expensive obstacle, calls to take them seriously may feel inauthentic, alienating and absurd.

Discussions about values require some seriousness if they are to resonate with their audience.

If, for example, a commencement speaker praising the value of artificial intelligence is met with jeers from graduates – as former Google CEO Eric Schmidt was in May 2026 – the speaker’s message is immediately rendered inert.

These students’ jeers fell short of offering an argument against the speaker’s claims; instead, they created an atmosphere that prevented those claims from receiving consideration. For graduates pessimistic about AI’s implications for the labor market, claims professing its value feel inauthentic.

Together, their jeers not only provided an escape from what felt like an alienating and inauthentic message about the value of AI, but they also created a sense of solidarity through a shared suspension of seriousness.

Far from being unique to Mangione, this suspension of seriousness recurs throughout online meme culture.

The OceanGate implosion prompted similar memes, including one depicting a pod of orcas with the caption “The water is safe, send more billionaires.”

Even Charlie Kirk’s assassination became material. In a trend known as “Kirkification,” users superimposed his face onto images ranging from the Mona Lisa to women in bikinis, transforming a grim event into a shared absurdity.

In my assessment, Gen Z’s creation and circulation of memes offers an escape from otherwise serious conversations – for example, conversations about the value of the UnitedHealthcare CEO’s life. This may be especially true when demands to condemn Mangione appear to ignore inequities within an American health insurance system perceived as corrupt and unjust.

Although commentators often dismiss Gen Z’s humor as nonsensical or nihilistic meme slop, scholarship suggests that it acts as a collaborative coping mechanism, driven by a desire for authenticity.

Memes about Mangione, or even campus lookalike contests centered on him, fall short of offering a precise moral argument in favor of largely suspending seriousness.

This style of humor can be seen in Mangione’s alleged decision to leave a backpack containing Monopoly money in Central Park. It was seen, too, on shell casings recovered after Kirk’s killing, which included video game commands, a sexually suggestive internet saying and “if you read this you are gay lmao.”

With the help of approximately a dozen undergraduate students, I examined the psychological and situational factors associated with Gen Z’s reactions to Mangione and other events – like Kirk’s assassination and the Kamala Harris is “Brat” phenomenon during the 2024 presidential election – in two studies currently under review.

Our findings indicate that favorable attitudes toward Mangione were associated not only with superficial factors, such as his perceived attractiveness, but also with higher levels of political cynicism.

Perceived systemic bias in the American justice system, for example, was addressed in a meme depicting Mangione walking into court with the text “You can kill dozens of kids and get a lesser sentence because their lives don’t matter as much as a CEO’s.” Federal prosecutors were seeking the death penalty against Mangione for a charge a judge dismissed in January 2026.

Casting Gen Z’s reactions as nihilistic obscures the values and institutional distrust connected to them and fails to appreciate their egalitarian and pragmatic ideals. Dismissing them may deepen the alienation that allowed the death of a father of two to become a joke.

Although political commentators disagree about how to interpret the response to Mangione, many accept a seemingly basic principle: Killing should never be justified.

Yet decades of research on moral judgment shows that people do not apply that principle consistently. Instead, in certain situations, like in the famous “trolley problem,” people frequently judge killing to be morally permissible – especially when that killing is expected to promote the well-being of others.

Simplistic and sweeping moral injunctions not only fail to appreciate people’s actual moral attitudes, but they also eliminate the possibility of having authentic and nuanced conversations.

Those conversations need not end by endorsing Mangione as a sympathetic figure. However, an open and authentic conversation about Mangione cannot be realized in spaces that require all discussion of the event to be reduced to affirmations that, as has been advocated by some, “Murder is bad. Period.”

Such requirements can make conversations about significant moral issues – even controversial ones, like the morality of Mangione’s alleged actions – little more than demands for conformity. In this case, those boundaries risk ignoring and, thus, further alienating, Gen Z.

Gen Z’s humor shows that almost anything can become a joke. I believe the danger of that is not that young people reject values, but that continued alienation may leave them laughing when seriousness is most required.
news.summary: Having grown up with smartphones and social media, this generation has come of age in an increasingly online world

news.text:
To give you a sense of it, consider Darializa Avila Chevalier, one of the DSA members to win a Democrat primary. “F!@# Kamala Harris” she tweeted when Harris was vice president. A year prior she’d called Joe Biden a “rapist”. When Chevalier won her New York primary, a former Bill Clinton aide said the party “should not seat her in the caucus” because she is “not a democrat”. But he also lit a fire under progressives who sought a takeover of their own, and took inspiration from Bernie Sanders. When Trump first entered office, the DSA had an influx of tens of thousands of new, young members. That plateaued when Biden became president, but Trump’s second victory has brought the energy back. And this energy isn’t just threatening to transform the Democrats. It’s transforming the very DSA that is currently besieging it.

The DSA was established in the ’80s with the aim of pulling the Democratic Party in a more progressive direction. It was socialist – committed to bringing about the end of capitalism – but also anti-communist. It upheld liberty, free speech, and free elections. It specifically banned communists from becoming members. But the post-Trump influx contained a new hardcore of genuine communists and Marxist-Leninists. The past decade has been one of internal DSA ructions, with some of its founding members leaving in protest. One Marxist-Leninist faction, called the Red Star caucus, now boasts that “nearly half” of the members of the DSA’s highest leadership body “openly identify as communists”. Meanwhile, the DSA officially removed its ban on communist members.

As a result, the DSA is now divided in its aims. One group retains the old vision of influencing the Democrats. Another wants to establish a separate party and fight them. news.title: Jill Biden Says She Doesn't Think She'll See a Female President in Her Lifetime — and Admits Being 'Shocked' Kamala Harris Lost to Trump
news.text:
Jill Biden doesn't think she will see a female president in her lifetime, RadarOnline.com can reveal, less than two years after she watched Donald Trump defeat Kamala Harris in the presidential election.

The former First Lady appeared on SiriusXM’s Let's Talk Off Camera with Kelly Ripa and discussed whether a woman will ever be Commander-in-Chief.'I Feel Like Probably Not in My Lifetime'"Do you think we'll ever see a woman president in our lifetimes?" the talk show host asked Jill, as she responded, "In my lifetime? I'm 75. I feel like probably not in my lifetime, Kelly, but maybe in yours."

Jill then recalled Harris' unexpected loss to Trump, and noted, "I really did think last time that Kamala was gonna win. I was out on the campaign trail for her. I saw the excitement, I saw the crowds, I saw it at the convention. 

"I saw all the energy, and I thought, 'Finally, we're going to have a woman president.'"

The 75-year-old added, "And I must tell you, I was shocked the morning after when I got up at 5:00 in the morning to feed Willow and get ready for the day, and I found out that she had lost. Shocked."Jill Biden V. Kamala HarrisJill, who previously suggested Harris "would be a good president," is rumored to have had a feud with the ex-veep behind the scenes.

In her memoir, View From the East Wing, Jill touches on the moment her husband, Joe Biden, decided to step down from the presidency. During an interview, journalist Paola Ramos shared, "There's this one moment in the book that I think a lot of people are talking about, when you describe that when President Biden was talking about stepping down and endorsing her, you walk out. You walk out of the room because she wanted an immediate endorsement, and you storm out."

However, Jill pushed back on Ramos' choice of words, responding, "I didn't say storm... Joe had made the decision to drop out. It was very emotional, you might well imagine." Harris would end up taking over for Joe and battling it out against Trump.

In Harris' memoir, 107 Days, she noted the lack of support she felt she received from Jill and Joe and their inner circle while running in 2024.'I Want It Sooner'"And when the stories were unfair or inaccurate, the president's inner circle seemed fine with it... It seemed as if they decided I should be knocked down a little bit more," she claimed in her book. According to Harris, it was Jill who pushed her husband to stay in the race following his disastrous debate performance against Trump.

She noted, "It's Joe and Jill's decision. We all said that, like a mantra, as if we'd all been hypnotized. Was it grace, or was it recklessness? In retrospect, I think it was recklessness."

Joe dropped out on July 21, 2024, and in her memoir, Jill claimed Harris was eager for an endorsement, as she allegedly said, "Oh my God, Joe. Are you sure?"

After Joe made it clear he wanted to wait until morning to endorse her, Jill claimed Harris demanded, "I want it sooner."According to Jill, after her husband said he'd give Harris a call "when I figure this out," she allegedly pressed him, "Could you do it soon? Say, in 20 minutes?" 

Harris' behavior led Jill to leave the room. The 61-year-old has not confirmed whether she will be running for president, as according to sources, "She hasn’t ruled it out. No credible strategist would recommend ruling it out this early.

"But she also understands that the window to make the case that her vision and leadership in elected office is what this moment requires isn't open indefinitely."
news.summary: Jill Biden has admitted she doesn't think America will elect a female president in her lifetime.

news.title: Trump-supporting Miss North Carolina USA STRIPPED of title over problematic posts
news.text:
The group behind the Miss North Carolina USA contest says the decision to strip the title from 27-year-old Brittany Boltinhouse was a "difficult" one.

The Mexican-Honduran model from Beulaville posted messages years ago that the organization said went against its values. 

She had warned that voting for Kamala Harris would risk turning America into a 'third world country.'

Boltinhouse is also a supporter of President Donald Trump, though that wasn't included in the organization's statement.

"This decision was not made lightly," the organizers said on Instagram. "It followed a thorough review of recently surfaced information and was based on the totality of the circumstances and our responsibility to preserve the integrity of the Miss North Carolina USA title and the values of our organization."

The posts were not included, but the NC Beat documented that Boltinhouse used the N-word numerous times between 2017 and 2018, and referred to herself as "toxic."

She had warned that voting for Kamala Harris would risk turning America into a "third world country" in another post and also shared a photograph of herself at a Trump rally, according to the Beat.

The discovery led to backlash from some who objected to her posts and called her a "self-hating, Trump-supporting, racist, ignorant women [sic] who does not speak for me or for any of the other ACTUAL PROUD HISPANAS." 

Miss USA Chairman and CEO Thom Brodeur said that "racism, homophobia, transphobia, [and] language that strips any person of their dignity" are against the organization's values, but it's unclear if he was referring to her posts or her support of the president. 

"As an organization entrusted with selecting and preparing women to represent our states on the national stage," the organization continued, "we must uphold the standards and values that our titleholders agree to embrace when accepting the honor of wearing the crown."

The incident is even more bizarre considering that Trump once owned the Miss USA pageant before he became president.

Myla Hadley, the runner-up in the pageant contest, will take up the mantle of Miss North Carolina USA 2026.

news.title: EXCLUSIVE: Inside Trump's Feuds With Pop Stars After Katy Perry Joined Hit List
news.text:
Donald Trump is still locked in a new front in his long campaign of cultural combat – a rolling war against some of the world's biggest pop stars, whose music he borrows for his own political ends while publicly deriding them when they push back.

As RadarOnline.com readers know, the US president, 80, is now waging war in Iran and threatening invasions of Canada, Greenland, Cuba, Colombia and Panama, and has also ordered strikes in Syria, Somalia, Iraq, Yemen and Nigeria. 

But some of his most personal battles have played out not on foreign soil but in the glare of the entertainment world, as he clashes with Katy Perry, Taylor Swift, Bruce Springsteen, Madonna, Beyoncé – and a long list of other musicians who have denounced his policies or blocked him from using their songs.Katy Perry Clashes With TrumpPerry was thrust into Trump's crosshairs last week after the White House used her 2010 hit Firework as the soundtrack to a video montage of military strikes titled "Iran has been warned."

As Perry sang "Boom! Boom! Boom!," the video showed bombs exploding. 

She said: "To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponised to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for."

Perry added her music was supposed to be "for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare."

The 41-year-old singer's comments have sparked a fresh round of presidential recriminations.

Trump removed Firework from his video – only to retaliate by posting footage of Perry in military fatigues holding a weapon, spliced between images of Trump and fighter jets. 

The rage came as the clip, taken from one of Perry's old music videos, was repurposed to suggest she was aligned with his hardline stance. 

A senior political source exclusively told Radar: "If Katy Perry wants to lecture us about peace, she shouldn't be surprised when we remind people she once played a soldier on screen."Taylor Swift Draws Trump's FurySwift's decision to endorse Democratic candidate Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential race marked another turning point in Trump's war on music's biggest names. 

After months of publicly courting the singer's vote, Trump erupted online: "I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!" 

He posted the outburst on social media, and has also raged online: "Has anyone noticed that, since I said 'I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,' she's no longer 'HOT?'" This came despite Swift headlining a record-breaking world tour and releasing blockbuster albums. 

One Harris campaign aide said: "Trump went from begging for her approval to belittling her success the moment she chose democracy over him."

Beyoncé has also become a target. 

Trump falsely claimed she had been paid $10million to endorse Harris and appear at a 2024 rally in Houston, Texas, alleging the performer "left the stage to a booing and angry audience" – even though her event company received only $165,000 to cover costs and video evidence showed no jeering. 

Trump escalated the feud last year, saying Beyoncé and every celebrity who backed Harris "should all be prosecuted." 

A source close to Beyoncé said: "Trump tries to criminalise dissent – if you're not singing for him, he wants you silenced."More Stars Hit BackThe pattern extends beyond those who criticise him outright.

The White House used Puerto Rican rapper Bad Bunny's song La Mudanza in a video showing federal agents handcuffing immigrants, in a move insiders acknowledge was designed to antagonise the Super Bowl headliner.

Trump called the artist "absolutely terrible, one of the worst, EVER," and "an affront to the Greatness of America," complaining by singing in Spanish, "nobody understands a word this guy is saying," despite tens of millions of Spanish speakers in the US alone.

Other stars have reacted angrily when their songs surfaced in Trump's output.

Ariana Grande was outraged when her track Bye backed a White House video of immigration arrests.

She wrote on social media: "Please do not ever use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense."

Sabrina Carpenter saw her song Juno turned into a soundtrack to another immigration clip, branding it "evil and disgusting." She added: "Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda."

Kesha called the White House administration "perverts" in February after her 2011 song Blow appeared on a Trump TikTok video of missile strikes titled Lethality.White House Defends StrategyOne Washington insider told us: "By provoking stars and leaning on their work without permission, Trump and his team court outrage and viral attention – it's a classic bid to try and stay relevant across all age groups online."

White House communications director Steven Cheung said: "All these 'singers' keep falling for this. This just gives us more attention and more view counts to our videos because people want to see what they're bitching about." 

Our Washington insider added: "For Trump, the backlash from pop royalty is just another battlefront – and the noise is part of the strategy."
news.summary: The list of Donald Trump's feuds with pop stars has been growing after Katy Perry joined the list.
news.author: Aaron Tinney

news.title: Trump team to hand out $3B in ‘BIDEN’ grants – for communities that help deport more migrants
news.text:
The Department of Justice is making $3 billion available in grants to communities that agree to cooperate with federal immigration forces carrying out President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

The Bridging Immigration-related Deficits Experienced Nationwide (or, BIDEN) Program was established – and spitefully named after former president Joe Biden – in last year's One Big Beautiful Bill, making the money available for distribution through September 2028.

One of the biggest offerings ever made by the DOJ, according to The Washington Post, the program is intended to bolster immigration enforcement by encouraging greater cooperation between state and federal authorities.

A 21-page introductory document explains that the funding is intended for "locating and apprehending aliens who have committed a crime under federal, state, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States."

Jurisdictions that apply for the money have to agree to "fully participate" in the ICE 287(g) partnership, which brings together local police forces with immigration agents, and with the Homeland Security Task Force.

However, should their applications prove successful, they may spend their grant at their own discretion, so long as it goes towards hiring and training law enforcement personnel, investing in new crimefighting technology such as drones, body cameras and surveillance systems and building new temporary detention centers.

Jurisdictions do not need to prove that they were harmed directly by Biden administration immigration policies in order to qualify, only demonstrate a willingness to support Trump-backed enforcement efforts.

They will, however, be expected to commit to reimbursing "the costs associated with federal law enforcement intervention" should that later become necessary "to reduce crime or public disorder" related to the crackdown.

"This Department of Justice is committed to ensuring Biden-era border disasters never happen again," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in a statement introducing the program, underlining the highly partisan nature of the offering.

"We are proud to once again champion law and order."

Former New Jersey attorney general Matthew Platkin, a Democrat, scorned the strategy, telling the Post: "Even the name of the grant itself is a political statement that is holding critical funds hostage to achieve goals they haven't been able to through legal means.

"It's a slap in the face to law enforcement."

The DOJ issued its first call for applications last month and has further funding rounds planned for August and September.

The department says it has already received 181 applications in the first 30 days, according to the Post, which considers that a slow start given the generosity of the offering but says that demand is likely to pick up over the coming months.

Trump was returned to power in November 2024 promising mass deportations, scaremongering during the campaign about "migrant crime" and pet-eating Haitians in Ohio and blaming Biden and Kamala Harris for allowing in "stone-cold killers."

Immigration and Customs Enforcement was subsequently greatly expanded under the leadership of former Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem and sent into Democrat-run cities such as Los Angeles and Chicago to round-up people suspected of being in the country illegally, inspiring widespread protests and a slew of negative stories about its activities.

However, the deaths of two protesters during Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis in January forced a rethink, with Noem and Border Patrol chief Greg Bovino removed and border czar Tom Homan placed in overall charge.

Noem was replaced by Oklahoma Republican senator Markwayne Mullin, who has already reportedly been the subject of "growing tensions" with the White House after ordering ICE to pause traffic stops following the deaths of two more people in Maine and Texas.
news.author: Joe Sommerlad

news.title: The Left’s Fake Conversion To Religious Liberty
news.text:
The progressive legal establishment for years treated religious freedom exemptions as obstacles to be dismantled, threatening the livelihoods, consciences, and institutions of Christian business owners, healthcare workers, and even nuns.

Now, the left is embracing the very religious-liberty arguments it spent years working to defeat.

Religious exemptions have typically rested on one of two legal foundations: the First Amendment’s protection of religious exercise or the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which requires the government to justify substantial burdens on religious practice under the strictest level of judicial scrutiny.

This shift on the left is not merely rhetorical. Hoosier Jews for Choice has sued for religious exemptions from Indiana’s abortion ban, arguing that the law conflicts with Jewish teachings about when life begins. The Latino Christian National Network and other Christian and Jewish organizations have invoked religious freedom in challenges to ICE enforcement near houses of worship and in efforts to protect faith groups that shelter illegal immigrants.

Safehouse, a Philadelphia nonprofit, is likewise pressing a religious-liberty claim for permission to operate a supervised drug-consumption site. The organization argues that its Judeo-Christian obligation to preserve life and care for the sick entitles it to an exemption from federal drug laws. Together, the cases show progressive organizations adopting the same legal protections their political allies have long sought to narrow when invoked by conservative Christians, according to The Guardian. 

Constitutional and policy scholars, however, told the Caller the sudden pivot isn’t a genuine defense of conscience — it’s a tactical workaround that falls apart under legal scrutiny. (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: Trump’s DOJ Sues Blue County Over Gun Ban In Churches)

Josh Blackman, a constitutional law professor at South Texas College of Law Houston, told the Caller that many of the cases are “silly and cynical,” but legally shrewd.

He said the strategy emerged as it became clear the Supreme Court would overturn Roe v. Wade in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, returning abortion policy to the states.

“Abortion is so important to the left, they had to find some way of protecting it, and they’ll use whatever tools are available,” Blackman said. “They replaced due process with an appeal to religion.”

Blackman added that the claims also give progressives a way to accuse conservatives of hypocrisy for supporting religious-liberty protections in earlier cases while questioning their use now.

Many earlier religious-liberty cases involved objections to government compulsion: a Christian baker declining to create a cake for a same-sex wedding, for example, or nuns resisting a mandate to provide contraceptive coverage.

The newer cases, by contrast, use religious-liberty claims to advance policy outcomes their proponents already supported on secular grounds. That distinction has led legal scholars such as Blackman to question whether the newfound commitment to religious freedom is principled or merely strategic.

Blackman, who has followed the Jewish abortion litigation for four years, said the plaintiffs may struggle to establish both the sincerity of their asserted beliefs and standing to sue — particularly where some of the women bringing the cases are not pregnant.

But, Blackman noted, “the problem is courts are very, very hesitant to probe sincerity.”

“The left is throwing everything against the wall to see what sticks,” Ethics and Public Policy Center President Ryan T. Anderson told the Caller, adding that “they have unfortunately not developed any newfound respect for religious freedom.”

Anderson said the left’s religious liberty claims are hardly comparable to those of the baker or nun, and instead “make a mockery of religious liberty.”

He compared the effort to self-described Satanists who claim a religious liberty right to obtain abortions, adding that “the attempts to use religious liberty protections to attack basic human rights protections for the unborn should be as successful as religious liberty claims to kill any other class of human beings.”

Anderson said many of the progressive religious liberty claims are opportunistic, noting that “they will ultimately fail either because the purported religious belief is not sincere or because the government has a truly compelling interest being pursued in the least restrictive way.”

The left’s new strategy marks a sharp departure from its earlier efforts to force religious groups to yield to progressive policy priorities, including repeated attempts to pass the Do No Harm Act across six consecutive Congresses — an effort championed in part by Kamala Harris during her Senate tenure.

The bill would have barred individuals and organizations from invoking RFRA to seek exemptions from federal laws governing civil rights, employment, healthcare and other areas where advocates argued religious claims could enable discrimination. Harris said the First Amendment’s guarantee of religious freedom should “never be used to undermine other Americans’ civil rights or subject them to discrimination on the basis of race, gender, sexual orientation, or gender identity.”

The legislative push followed a major setback for progressives in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, in which the Supreme Court ruled that certain corporations could not be compelled under the Affordable Care Act to provide contraceptive coverage if doing so would violate their religious beliefs.

After failing to substantially narrow those protections through Congress, progressive advocates are now turning to the courts to invoke the same religious-liberty doctrines on behalf of abortion access, immigration sanctuaries and supervised drug-consumption sites.

While the left’s legal strategy may have changed, Anderson said its underlying goals have not “evolved,” pointing to New York state’s recent effort to force Roman Catholic nuns to participate in assisted suicide.

Blackman said most of the cases appear to be political or philosophical disputes recast in religious terms. Still, some could succeed if courts are reluctant to apply religious-liberty protections less generously to progressive plaintiffs than they did to conservatives in earlier cases. (RELATED: FBI, DEA Withhold Court-Ordered Files On Nigerian President’s Alleged Drug Trafficking Ahead Of Trump Meeting)

Progressive plaintiffs now stand on the opposite side of a religious-liberty debate that has divided the left and right for more than a decade. Their lawsuits will test how broadly protections once associated with conservative causes apply when invoked in pursuit of progressive ones.
news.summary: ‘A mockery of religious liberty’
